title: Domain or Tenant Policy Modification: Group Policy Modification
shortTitle: Domain or Tenant Policy Modification: Group Policy Modifi...
summary: Group Policy modification is the Active Directory branch of policy abuse. A Group Policy Object is a directory object linked to sites, domains or organisational units, and its settings are stored as files under the domain share in the SYSVOL folder. Any principal with write permission on the object or on the policy template files can add a preference, a logon script, a service setting or a scheduled task that the affected computers apply on their next policy refresh. Detection rests on the fact that the object itself records who changed it and when, that preference files keep version numbers used to trigger client refresh, and that the resulting execution appears on endpoints as a child of the policy engine rather than of a user. Security filtering and new link targets are common tells, because they redirect the new setting to selected victims.

beginner.definition: This is a specific kind of central rule change. Group Policy Objects, usually shortened to GPOs, are the containers that hold settings for Windows computers in a company network. An attacker with write permission edits a GPO so it delivers something harmful. This sub-technique is the Group Policy part of the wider domain policy modification technique you meet first.
beginner.whyItMatters: Group Policy runs with high trust on every machine it reaches. A single edited GPO can add a task that runs as an administrator on many computers at once. It also survives reboots, so the attacker keeps a foothold without touching each machine. Administrators change GPOs often, which makes a quiet malicious edit easy to hide among normal work. Knowing who may edit which GPO is your main defence.
howItWorks: The attacker obtains write permission on a Group Policy Object, or on the files behind it.
They attach to the directory service and open the object for editing with a normal management tool.
They add a harmful setting, often a scheduled task or a startup script, to the policy files.
They raise the policy version numbers so client computers notice the change and apply it.
The computers read the new setting at their next refresh and run what the attacker placed there.
Some attackers narrow the policy so it only applies to the machines they care about.
beginner.example: Imagine a block of flats where the caretaker posts printed instructions in a shared hallway cupboard. Residents check that cupboard every morning. If a stranger quietly swaps one page for a note saying leave your door unlocked, the residents may follow the new note without asking who wrote it. The cupboard is trusted, the paper looks the same, and only the version number on the corner shows the page was changed.
takeaways: Treat the ability to edit a GPO as equivalent to administrator rights on every machine it reaches.
Policy version numbers and new links are useful signs that a GPO was changed outside process.
Monitor who edits policies and record the object identifiers involved.

objectives: Explain what a Group Policy Object is and where its settings are stored.
State how this sub-technique differs from the wider domain policy modification technique.
Describe at least three harmful things an attacker can deliver through a modified policy.
Identify the records that show a policy object was edited and by which account.
Explain how security filtering and new links can direct a harmful policy at chosen hosts.
Explain why policy changes survive reboots and reinstalls of individual machines.
